nodes.label: Methodology
nodes.question: What methodological approach does the study use to analyze waste re-utilization economies?
nodes.answer: The study offers a comparative analysis using load capacity factors as an alternative proxy to demonstrate the shape of the load capacity curve (LCC) in specified economies.
nodes.paragraph: The European Union recently declared that half of total emissions come from daily wastage by productive & non- productive activities. In such a scenario, the circular economy has become the last resort to solve this issue by efficiently allocating wastage in energy production 21. This initiative not only tries to secure the environmental quality but also fills-out the energy shortage. The current study aims to describe the overall environmental challenges (income, urbanization & natural resources) and their best solutions (renewable energy, ICT & circular economy) for the top waste re-utilize economies (WRE) from 2000 to 2021. It is imperative to introduce this study S contribution to existing literature properly. Firstly , this study considers income a determinant of environmental degradation because most economies have tried to speed up their development plans to compete with other nations at any cost of negative externalities. It S a common belief that economies damage their available natural and other resources connected with sustainability and development plans, bringing severe environmental deterioration with rapid economic growth. Also, the present study offers a comparative analysis by using the load capacity factors as an alternative proxy of explained variables to demonstrate the shape of the load capacity curve (LCC) in specified economies.

nodes.question: What aspects of sustainability does the study explore concerning waste management practices?
nodes.answer: The study explores waste management practices informed by local knowledge that support ecological system sustainability.
nodes.paragraph: This theory highlights the social, political and economic factors that influence ecological outcomes. Building on the foundations of social ecology theory, the socio-ecological systems (SES) framework provides a com- prehensive approach for examining waste dynamics within households, between households, and between household solid waste generators and the natural environment. This study explores waste management practices informed by local knowledge that support ecological system sustain- ability. The SES framework helps to identify key variables needed to understand both social and ecological systems, and how they interact with each other (Binder et al. 2013 , p. 15 of 20). By suggesting specific variables, the framework allows us to analyze the potential for sustainable develop- ment within these systems, providing a structured way to assess whether a social-ecological system can remain resil- ient and sustainable over time (Ostrom 2009, p. 420; Leslie et al. 2015, p. 5979). nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Why is finding more sustainable waste management practices considered crucial?
nodes.answer: It is crucial because current methods threaten key sectors such as tourism and occupy valuable land that could otherwise be used for other purposes.
nodes.paragraph: Local and indigenous knowledge refers to the understand- ings, skills and philosophies developed by societies with long histories of interaction with their natural surroundings (Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change 2022, p. 817; Wheeler and Root Bernstein 2020, p. 1635); and often per - tains to ecological knowledge, management practices and customary institutions (Berkes 2012, p. 18). In line with the aim, the purpose of this study is to propose alternative approaches for achieving sustainable household solid waste management through integration of local knowledge. To achieve this purpose, the study raises the following research question: How can local knowledge contribute to sustainable household solid waste management in Borakalalo ward in Molepolole, Botswana? Guided by the research question, the objective of this study is to identify specific local practices used by households that promote a harmonious relation- ship between society and nature, contributing to sustainable waste management. nodes.label: Facts
nodes.question: Why was Lagos State selected for the research on SMEs and circular economy practices?
nodes.answer: Lagos State was selected because it is the most populous city in Nigeria and is currently facing challenges with its waste management systems, making it a relevant location for exploring the experiences and challenges of SMEs in implementing circular economy practices.
nodes.paragraph: The social, environmental, and economic benefits of a circular economy cannot be overemphasized. nodes.label: Management
nodes.question: What challenges are faced by SMEs in Nigeria regarding the implementation of circular economy and environmental sustainability practices?
nodes.answer: SMEs in Nigeria face challenges such as a lack of knowledge and skills, inadequate waste management systems, and difficulties in adopting effective environmental sustainability and circular economic activities.
nodes.paragraph: Through the introduction of innovative approaches, the circular economy enables employment creation and fosters economic growth and develop - ment. Significant benefits can be gained from a country implementing circular or sustainable practices, par - ticularly in terms of environmental benefits. Circular - ity helps devise effective strategies to overcome loss of resources, and emissions reduction, thereby protect - ing the ecosystem (Rizos et al., 2016). Circularity as a strategic model ensures the value of products, materi - als, and resources is maintained in the economy for as long as possible. All output from one process is input for another (see Fig. 1). Thus, a move towards a circular economy entails reducing the intake of virgin materials and reducing the generation of waste. At its core, the ethos of circularity is entrenched in the need to turn waste into wealth. The economic, environ - mental, and societal benefits of a circular economy are becoming increasingly evident. It presents businesses and governments all over the world with the potential to cre - ate an economy that is distributed, diverse, and inclusive.
